findings.finding: 0% of trades were accepted even though the listener got it wrong; 4 of 45 words in use now started as a mistake (misheard, or coined for something else).
findings.evidence: Oakhollow "me" = wood: coined for "two" by Gil (generation 1) · Ironcrag "me" = wood: coined for "two" by Gil (generation 1) · Saltmere "zuru" = planks: misheard: zulu → zuru (generation 25)

findings.q: Do the words used most change least?
findings.finding: Use vs. replacement rate across meanings: ρ = -0.47, p = 0.121, n = 12. Most used: two (6% replaced per generation), tools (35% replaced per generation), wood (13% replaced per generation); least: four (43%), five (59%).
findings.evidence: Real languages show this (Pagel et al. 2007). n = meanings, so treat as suggestive.

findings.q: Do a few families take over, and does the language narrow with them?
findings.finding: 2 founding families still alive. Families alive vs. distinct words per meaning across towns: ρ = 0.55, p = 0.004, n = 25.
findings.evidence: Children go to the best-placed parents, so lineages die out: a founder effect, as in population genetics. Caution: families and variety both fall over time, so the correlation may be the language converging, not the families narrowing it.
